The four instruments measure genuinely independent physical quantities (not the same pendulum period or resonator frequency); cross-correlation failure is expected and requires no explanation.

Calibration baselines were not re-validated after Day 10; post-baseline data drift or scale relative to baseline in unknown ways, breaking cross-instrument agreement without affecting individual stream stability.

The Day 14 excursion in pendulum_lab (trials 173–178, mean 1.6626, min 1.6424) is a real, transient perturbation (mechanical, thermal, or procedural) specific to that instrument; it may point to a latent fragility affecting the instrument's accuracy in ways not yet visible in mean drift statistics.

The four instruments are not synchronized in their measurement timing, environmental sensitivity, or data-acquisition phase; they are drifting into and out of phase in ways that produce spurious near-zero correlations even if underlying physics is coherent.

At least one of the four instruments is miscalibrated, non-linear, or measuring an artifact (electronic noise, mechanical coupling to environmental vibration, or systematic bias in observation protocol) rather than the intended physical quantity.

Today's Day 34 readings reflect a genuine, real-time perturbation to the physical system (thermal transient, seismic event, environmental shock, or induced vibration) that affected all four instruments simultaneously or in rapid succession, not a calibration or instrumental failure.

The Day 34 excursion reflects a procedural or operational anomaly (observer fatigue, protocol drift, instrument-handling error, or environmental monitoring failure) that biased all four measurement streams in the same session, without implying underlying calibration or instrumental failure.

The Day 34 spike in variance is real but the underlying cross-instrument incoherence (near-zero correlations across all pre-Day 34 data) persists because the four instruments measure genuinely independent physical quantities or are mechanically decoupled by design; today's excursion does not resolve, and does not need to resolve, the lack of cross-stream agreement.

One or more instruments were miscalibrated at baseline (Days 1–10) or have suffered a slow, undetected gain or zero-offset drift that is not visible in z-score tests but corrupts cross-instrument agreement; the Day 34 spike may reflect the same underlying calibration fragility becoming acute.

The Day 34 variance spike is an artifact of incomplete data logging, sensor saturation, or data-acquisition buffer overflow on that day; readings are corrupted but appear internally consistent due to artifact repetition or correlated noise injection.

Day 40 variance spike is a transient environmental perturbation (thermal, seismic, vibration, or power transient) affecting all four instruments simultaneously; persistent cross-instrument incoherence reflects genuine instrumental independence or mechanical decoupling.

The four instruments are subject to chronic calibration drift or zero-offset errors established at baseline that were not detected by z-score tests; cross-instrument incoherence reflects miscalibration, not independence. Day 40 spike signals calibration system entering nonlinearity or saturation.

The four instruments genuinely measure independent physical quantities (e.g., separate pendulums, separate resonators, or different physical observables); zero cross-correlation is expected and normal. Day 40 spike reflects a procedural or environmental anomaly that happens to affect all four independent systems in parallel.

Day 40 variance spike is real and reflects either a procedural/observer anomaly (protocol drift, late timer-stopping, phase-sampling error) or data-acquisition malfunction (buffer overflow, sensor saturation, incomplete logging); cross-instrument incoherence is a separate, pre-existing issue.

Residual: unknown mechanism or unconsidered interaction (e.g., nonlinear coupling between instruments via shared mounting, environmental feedback loop, instrumental self-heating or thermal runaway, or a systematic error in cross-correlation methodology).
